reader.title: Fargo manhunt for Knudson (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of Fargo citizens hunted a Norwegian man, Knudson, intending to lynch him for a policeman's killing that a woman then confessed to; no one was harmed and no Black person appears in any account (A6, A7, A12, A15).

Citizens, described as 'a large force' and 'a mob', searched for Knudson meaning to lynch him for the policeman's death, but he was never caught and nobody was killed (A6, A12, A15). It was a threatened lynching of a man described as Norwegian (A6, A7).

The Yankton Press and Dakotaian's Fargo dispatch, the Chicago Times item and a separate eastern wire item each independently report the hunt for Knudson and the intent to lynch him (A6, A12, A15), and many dispatches agree on Mrs. Bunkle's confession and discharge (A1, A2, A18).

summary.text: The Fargo manhunt for Knudson was a search by townspeople of Fargo, Dakota Territory, on the night of July 5, 1882, for a Norwegian man they meant to lynch as the killer of Policeman Fred D. Alderman.
Knudson was not found, and by morning a woman, Mrs. Martin Bunkle, had confessed that she shot the officer after taking him for a tramp.
Papers outside Dakota noted that the crowd would have hanged an innocent man.
According to a Fargo dispatch, Knudson had been arrested for drunkenness and held in the city lockup, then released to find money for his fine on his promise to return.
When he did not come back, Alderman, who had been on the Fargo force a little over two months after serving as a policeman at Brainerd, went looking for him after dark.
Near the Grandin steamboat dock, Alderman knocked at a house he apparently took for Knudson's, but it belonged to Mrs. Martin Bunkle, whose husband had gone to Grafton and left her a revolver.
Mrs. Bunkle said that a man demanded entry about midnight, would not give his name and tried to break down the door, and that she fired, hitting him in the heart.
The first word in Fargo was that Knudson had shot Alderman while being arrested, and the city was described as in 'the wildest excitement'.
The Yankton Press and Dakotaian's correspondent wrote that a large force was searching 'every nook and corner' and that Knudson would be lynched at once if caught.
One eastern wire version added that the dying policeman had named Knudson's house as the source of the shot and that a mob hunted him all night.
Mrs. Bunkle gave herself up, confessed and was jailed, where she was reported to have given birth to a child.
A coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide and she was discharged.
No report of any action against the men who hunted Knudson, or of what became of him, was found.
Territorial and Midwestern dispatches of July 7, such as the Bismarck Tribune's 'Policeman Killed in Fargo', told the story as a policeman's death by mistake and did not mention the manhunt.
Wire briefs carried it east and west within days, often with garbled names such as 'Mrs. Runkle', 'Mrs. Burkle', 'Mrs. Bunker' and 'Mrs. Burke'.
The Yankton dispatch reported the coming lynching without comment and, in its later bulletin, said Mrs. Bunkle's story was not believed because hers was a 'low family' living in a 'low shanty'.

An item credited to the Chicago Times and headed 'Mrs. Bunkle's Deadly Aim' opened with the hunt and the statement that Knudson would have been lynched if caught, and it ran in roundups in Wisconsin, Minnesota and Dakota.
A shorter wire item, printed in New Jersey, called Knudson 'a bad character' but said the mob would have hanged an innocent man.

The earliest items, including a Wisconsin roundup, said a Norwegian named 'Knutzen' shot Alderman while resisting arrest, while later dispatches and the coroner's jury attributed the shooting to Mrs. Bunkle.

The Helena Herald dated the shooting 'last Tuesday' and said officers Alderman and Scott went to the house together, while the dispatches sent from Fargo at the time place it on Wednesday night, July 5, with Alderman alone.

accounts.gist: The dying policeman said the shot came from Jack Knudson's residence; a mob hunted him all night and would have hanged an innocent man.

framing.detail: Territorial and Midwestern dispatches headed 'Policeman Killed in Fargo' and 'Mistaken Identity' treated the case as a fatal mistake and did not mention the hunt.
The Yankton dispatch reported the coming lynching without comment, then said Mrs. Bunkle's story was 'not credited' because hers was a 'low family'.
The eastern wire item stressed that the mob 'would have hanged an innocent man'.

The July 5-6 dispatches are nearest the event.
